name: claim-check
intent: Keep messages small and the transport fast by moving a large or sensitive payload into a persistent store and letting the message carry only an opaque claim check that any participant can redeem to get the data back.
problem: Messages grow to carry documents, images, batch extracts or sensitive records, and the messaging system either rejects them, stores them at premium cost or slows down for every participant; intermediate steps that only route, filter or log must still carry the whole payload, and transport-level serialization, encryption and copying costs are paid at every hop.
context: Message-based integration over a transport with size or cost limits (queue and topic message caps, premium tiers for large messages, per-hop serialization) where only some processing steps actually need the payload, and where a store the participants can reach exists or can be operated - a file system, shared memory, database, blob or object store.
benefits: Messages stay small, so broker limits are respected and throughput, broker memory and paging behaviour stay stable under load.

The payload no longer travels through every intermediate step: routing, filtering, logging and monitoring components never deserialize it, which removes serialization, encryption and copy costs at each hop that does not need the data.

Payload confidentiality is decoupled from transport confidentiality: the data sits behind the store's access control, encryption and backup instead of travelling through queues, dead-letter channels and broker logs that unrelated operators can inspect.
Payload lifetime becomes explicit - TTL or claim-once deletion - so retention can be shorter than the messaging log, which lowers storage cost and the exposure window of sensitive data.
Total bytes moved fall for multi-hop flows: the payload is written once and read at the few places that need it instead of being copied along the whole route.
The wire contract shrinks to a small stable envelope, which decouples the routing schema from the payload schema and lets large payload formats evolve independently.
tradeoffs: Every consumer that needs the data pays an extra round trip to the store and inherits a new partial-failure mode: the message can arrive with its payload missing, expired, already claimed or forbidden.

The payload's lifecycle becomes the operator's problem - without an explicit deletion rule (synchronous on consumption, or an asynchronous reaper with retention limits) orphaned objects accumulate silently and the store grows faster than the traffic.

The claim check is the credential: a guessable or leaked token exposes the payload, so keys must be unguessable or signed, ideally scoped and expiring, and the store inherits the payload's confidentiality classification.

A transactional gap opens between storing the payload and sending the message; a crash in between leaks a payload nobody references or, in the other order, produces a message whose payload does not exist.
The message stops being self-describing: wire taps, message history, tracing and schema validation see only a token, so debugging and audit require joining the store with the message flow.

Two systems must be operated, secured, backed up and kept compatible (location, format, credentials, quotas, versioning), and a size threshold that bypasses the pattern for small messages creates two code paths every consumer must handle.
Every redeeming component needs store reachability and credentials, widening the trust boundary for participants that previously only needed the message and its headers.

participants.responsibility: Creates the message and holds the full payload; hands it to the Check Luggage step, or bypasses the pattern when the payload is small enough to travel inline.
Transformer at the seam that generates the unique claim check, writes the payload to the store, removes it from the message and puts the token in its place.
The only representation of the payload that crosses the transport: a unique, opaque, ideally signed and expiring key that names stored data without revealing anything about it.
Addressable, access-controlled, durable home of the payload (file system, shared memory segment, database, blob or object store) with an explicit retention and deletion rule.
Receives the reduced message, redeems the token through a Content Enricher style step, processes the payload and deletes it when the data may be claimed only once.

use_cases: Document and media pipelines where an image, video or PDF passes several stages but only some of them scan, index or transcode it.
Integration with a messaging system that caps message size or charges for large messages (Azure Service Bus, MSMQ, TIBCO, classic JMS brokers with small body limits).
Sensitive payloads that must not sit in queues, dead-letter channels or broker logs, and have to be protected by the store's ACLs, encryption and audit trail instead.
Long-running or multi-step workflows where the payload is needed at the beginning and at the end but not in between - routing, correlation and approval steps work on headers only.
B2B and EDI exchange where a batch or archive travels out of band while the protocol message carries only a reference to it.
Analytics and machine-learning pipelines that move feature sets or model artifacts between services while the queue carries job descriptors only.

Event-driven architectures with CQRS where large command or event payloads (e.g., audit logs, telemetry blobs, ML model artifacts) are externalized while the transport carries only the event envelope.
GDPR and data-residency scenarios where payload storage must live in a specific region or jurisdiction while the message routing infrastructure does not.
Multi-cloud or hybrid integrations where the payload store is reachable across network boundaries but the message broker is not.
Pastebin-style services where payload size (average 10 KB, p99 1 MB, hard cap 10 MB) exceeds DynamoDB's 400 KB item limit, requiring object storage for blobs and a metadata store for lookups.

AWS SQS messages above the 256 KB limit offloaded to S3 by the Amazon SQS Extended Client Library (Java/Python), which stores bodies up to 2 GB and transparently swaps the S3 pointer for the payload on send and receive.

NServiceBus endpoints whose oversized message properties travel via the Claim Check (DataBus) feature instead of the transport, with the payload kept in Azure Blob Storage, a file share or Redis and only the key in the message.
Azure Event Grid flows where uploading a payload to Blob Storage auto-generates the claim check in the notification event, so subscribers fetch the blob only when they actually intend to process it.
avoid_when: Messages are small: keep the payload inline, or apply the pattern conditionally behind a size threshold, because the store hop is pure latency and cost when the transport would have carried the message anyway.
Every step needs the payload - the pattern only pays off when at least one hop can skip the data; otherwise shrink the message with a Content Filter or Partial Response instead.
Nobody can own the store: without retention, deletion and access-control rules the pattern degenerates into an unbounded blob graveyard and a wider attack surface.
The transport already solves the problem (brokers with native large-message or tiered storage) or all participants already share a database that holds the payload by primary key.
Redemption cannot be made idempotent and the store cannot provide claim-once semantics, because a redelivery after a crash would process the payload twice.

The payload must be replayable from the message bus itself (e.g., Kafka log replay): a presigned-URL token embedded in an event expires and breaks replay after its TTL, unlike a stable URN that resolves forever.
anti_patterns: Claim check without a deletion rule: payloads are stored forever, so the store grows faster than the messaging traffic and every forgotten object stays a data-exposure risk.
Sequential or path-shaped tokens (order-4711, a raw file path, an incremental row id) instead of an unguessable or signed key, which makes the store enumerable to anyone who can see one message.
Consumers that parse the token structurally - assuming it is a path, a URL or a bucket key - instead of redeeming it through one seam, turning the store layout into a contract nobody can change.
Storing the payload externally but still shipping it in the message: double write, no benefit, and two copies that drift.
Redeeming the claim check in every processing step, which converts the store into a hot path and re-couples the flow to it - exactly the cost the pattern was meant to remove.
One shared store credential or one public container for all producers and tenants, so any participant can read every payload.

Embedding a presigned URL directly as the claim check token: the URL's expiry timestamp turns the message history into a time bomb, and the bearer capability leaks to every intermediate system that logs or queues the message.
No orphan-cleanup strategy: a crash between blob write and message publish leaves orphaned objects that accumulate silently, inflating storage costs and creating stale-data risk.
Storing payloads in the message broker itself for 'durability' when the broker's own tiered storage (e.g., Kafka remote tier via KIP-405) already provides the needed retention without the pattern.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: payload storage is a different concern from message routing and is handled by a different component.
Information hiding: only an opaque token crosses the wire; the store's location, format and credentials stay behind the redemption seam.
Loose coupling: producers and consumers need not agree on the payload encoding for routing, logging or filtering to work.
Single responsibility: the Check Luggage extracts and restores, consumers process, the store persists, and a retention rule (or reaper) deletes.
Least privilege: store access is granted only to the components that actually redeem, with the narrowest ACL and the shortest-lived credentials the store supports.

Optimistic storage: prefer a stable, opaque, non-expiring URN (e.g., UUIDv7 or signed token) over a credential-bearing URL (presigned URL, SAS token) as the token format, so the message history remains replayable without token-renewal logic.
best_practices: Make the claim check unique and unguessable - a UUID/ULID or a signed token with a purpose and an expiry - never a sequential id, a predictable path or a raw primary key.
Decide the payload lifecycle explicitly: claim-once on redemption or a retention/TTL rule plus a reaper, and monitor the store for objects whose message was processed long ago.
Write the payload to the store before publishing the message (or publish through an outbox) so a crash cannot emit a message whose payload does not exist.
Apply the pattern conditionally on a size threshold so small messages keep travelling inline and consumers are not forced through the store.
Keep the token opaque and redeem it in exactly one place; never let callers construct store keys themselves.
Grant the narrowest store credentials per component, encrypt payloads at rest where they are sensitive, and keep broker logs free of the data.
Correlate the token with the message id in logs and traces, and record deletions so operations can answer where a payload is and whether it still exists.
Make redemption idempotent, or use claim-once semantics with an explicit error for repeat claims, so redelivery cannot double-process a payload.
Include a payload checksum (SHA-256 or MD5) alongside the token so consumers can verify integrity on retrieval without trusting the store or the network.

Prefer an opaque URN token over a presigned URL: presigned URLs expire, break event replay (Kafka log replay, DLQ reprocess), and carry a bearer capability that leaks to every system touching the message. If you must use presigned URLs, mint them at retrieval time from a gateway that authenticates the caller, rather than embedding a long-lived credential in the message.

Use a three-layer TTL pipeline for blob cleanup: (1) S3 lifecycle rules or Azure Blob Lifecycle policies delete by TTL-prefix (handles 90%+ of cleanup with no custom code), (2) DynamoDB or metadata-table TTL auto-deletes index rows within days of expiry, (3) a daily reconciler sweeps orphaned blobs and dangling rows. The service layer checks expires_at on every read and returns 404 immediately regardless of physical deletion state.
Implement dead-letter handling for failed retrievals: after exhausting exponential-backoff retries, route to a DLQ rather than retrying indefinitely, to prevent message poison pill accumulation.
For fan-out scenarios (multiple consumers needing the same payload), use reference counting or a shared TTL lifecycle policy instead of per-consumer deletion, so late subscribers can still retrieve.
Instrument both the store and the broker: track store fetch latency, 404 rate (orphaned claim checks), and blob count growth rate as leading indicators of cleanup failures.

When using Kafka, consider Kafka's own tiered storage (KIP-405) for broker-side large message offloading before implementing an application-level claim-check, as it avoids the transactional gap problem entirely.

For multi-cloud scenarios, use a cloud-agnostic abstraction (e.g., Go CDK blob + pubsub in go-claimcheck, or Kafka Connect SMT with pluggable storage backend) so the storage backend can be swapped without changing the wire format.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Claim Check (Message Transformation chapter).
https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/patterns/messaging/StoreInLibrary.html
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/claim-check
https://docs.spring.io/spring-integration/reference/claim-check.html
Apache Kafka KIP-1159: Large message reference based Serializer (proposes a native LargeMessageSerializer using a PayloadStore abstraction, rejecting chunking due to complexity).

Apache Kafka KIP-405: Kafka Tiered Storage (enables remote tiered storage for brokers, reducing local storage dependence; relevant as an alternative to application-level claim-check for large messages).

Apache Kafka KIP-1248 / KIP-1254: Broker and Consumer support for remote tiered storage fetch (enables consumers to fetch directly from S3/HDFS rather than through the broker, with signed URL support).

https://github.com/bakdata/kafka-large-message-serde: A Kafka Serde that transparently stores large records in S3, Azure Blob Storage, or Google Cloud Storage and passes a reference in the Kafka message (formerly kafka-s3-backed-serde).

https://github.com/irori-ab/claim-check-interceptors: Java Kafka client library implementing Claim Check via interceptors for Azure Blob Storage and S3, with streaming mode for memory-efficient large payload handling.

https://github.com/peczenyj/go-claimcheck: Cloud-agnostic Go implementation powered by Go CDK, with pluggable blob storage (S3/GCS/Azure) and Pub/Sub (Kafka/RabbitMQ/SNS/SQS), rich metadata (checksums, size), and Zstd compression.

https://github.com/CokeLee777/kafka-connect-claim-check-smt: Kafka Connect Single Message Transform implementing Claim Check, offloading payloads to S3 or filesystem, with configurable size threshold.

James Carr, 'The Route Table Is the Contract: Claim Checks Behind a Gateway' (2026) - critical analysis of presigned URLs vs stable URNs in claim-check messages, and the gateway-as-authority pattern for secure retrieval.
Juraj Fiala, Distributed Application Architecture Patterns (DAAP) - Claim Check pattern reference implementation with formal applicability conditions and failure mode analysis.

https://stackpractices.com/patterns/claim-check-pattern/ (2026) - cloud implementation variants (S3 pre-signed URLs, shared volume, database BLOB, CDN, streaming), operational guidance, and broker comparison (Kafka 1MB, SQS 256KB, Service Bus 256KB/1MB).

https://thesystemguide.com/understanding-claim-check-design-pattern/ (2026) - payload lifecycle management strategies including synchronous deletion, asynchronous deletion, and conditional implementation thresholds.

https://developersvoice.com/blog/cloud-design-patterns/claim-check-pattern/ (2025) - .NET implementation with Azure Blob Storage and Azure Service Bus, SAS token security, dead-lettering, and lifecycle management.

https://www.donnchadh.dev/claims-check-pattern-a-strategy-for-handling-large-payloads-in-distributed-systems/ (2024) - SAP Integration patterns perspective on payload lifecycle, consistency concerns, and retry strategies.

https://granit-fx.dev/dotnet/architecture/patterns/claim-check/: Granit's IClaimCheckStore abstraction for .NET with typed extensions (StorePayloadAsync, ConsumePayloadAsync), soft DI dependency, and GDPR/ISO 27001 use case.

https://codingdroplets.com/claim-check-pattern-aspnet-core: ASP.NET Core perspective with a comparison table (without vs with claim-check) across broker message size, consumer latency, payload lifecycle, fan-out cost, failure domains, and testability.

https://hld.handbook.academy/curriculum/case-studies/pastebin/ (2026) - pastebin design case study demonstrating claim-check with DynamoDB metadata + S3 blob storage split, three-layer TTL pipeline (S3 lifecycle, DynamoDB TTL, reconciler), and write-order discipline.

https://www.ediverse.io/en/patterns/message-store/: Message Store pattern comparison - notes that Message Store shares object-store + index infrastructure with Claim Check and is distinguished by its audit/replay purpose rather than its storage mechanism.

https://juraf.github.io/daap/performance-and-latency-patterns/claim-check/: Formal DAAP reference with applicability conditions (size, sensitivity, intermediary need) and garbage-collection strategies.

https://github.com/awslabs/amazon-sqs-java-extended-client-lib: Official AWS extended client library (Java, with a Python variant) implementing Claim Check over SQS - payloads from 256 KB to 2 GB stored in S3 and referenced by pointer, with always-store or size-threshold modes.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-s3-messages.html: AWS developer guide on managing large Amazon SQS messages with the Extended Client Library and Amazon S3.

https://docs.particular.net/nservicebus/messaging/claimcheck/: NServiceBus Claim Check (DataBus) documentation - typed ClaimCheckProperty and convention-based claim-check properties, pluggable stores (Azure Blob, file share, Redis), and cleanup caveats.

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/2784703/jms-message-model-to-include-data-or-pointers-to-data: practitioner discussion of pointers vs full data in JMS messages - lost intermediate state and extra store access as the recurring criticisms of claim-check-style messaging.

https://www.nazarboyko.com/articles/building-event-driven-systems-with-aws (2023) - AWS event-driven pitfalls: claim check is 'not a free lunch' - extra S3 round trips per send/receive and more complex error handling; evaluate whether payload sizes actually necessitate the offload.
